questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a clustered and a nonclustered index?
options: A clustered index determines the table's physical row order and is the table itself (one per table); a nonclustered index is a separate structure of key columns plus a pointer back to the row (many per table)
A nonclustered index always contains every column in the table
A clustered index can only exist on a heap
There is no functional difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: The clustered index IS the table, physically ordered by its key; a nonclustered index is a separate, compact structure that points back to the full row.

options: The extra trip back to the clustered index to fetch columns that aren't present in a nonclustered index being used
The process of creating a primary key
A synonym for a table scan
A step that only happens during index creation, never during query execution
questions.explain: When a nonclustered index doesn't cover all the columns a query needs, SQL Server follows the pointer back to the clustered index per matching row — a Key Lookup.

questions.q: Given an index on `(CustomerId, OrderDate)`, which query can use it for an efficient seek, per the leftmost-prefix rule?
options: WHERE CustomerId = 4210 AND OrderDate >= '2026-01-01'
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' (with no filter on CustomerId)
WHERE OrderDate = '2026-01-01' OR CustomerId IS NULL
None of these queries can use the index
questions.explain: The leftmost-prefix rule means the index can be seeked using its leading column, or leading columns together — filtering on the trailing column alone cannot seek it.

questions.q: What does 'selectivity' measure, and why does it matter for index design?
options: The fraction of distinct values in a column relative to row count; high selectivity makes a column a strong index candidate, low selectivity often doesn't justify the write overhead
How recently a column was added to the table
Whether a column allows NULL values
The number of indexes currently defined on a table
questions.explain: A highly selective column (like a customer ID) lets a seek narrow to few rows; a low-selectivity column (like a 3-value status flag) usually isn't worth indexing as a leading key.

questions.q: A composite index is built as `(Status, CreatedDate)`, where Status has only 3 possible values. A query filters only on `CreatedDate >= @cutoff`. What happens, per this lesson?
options: The index generally cannot be seeked efficiently for this query, because CreatedDate is a trailing column and isn't a usable prefix on its own
SQL Server automatically reorders the index at query time to put CreatedDate first
The query will always fail with an error
The index becomes a clustered index automatically to compensate
questions.explain: Because CreatedDate is the second key column, filtering on it alone doesn't give the optimizer a usable prefix to seek on — the leading column has to be involved.
